# NPM Improved v1.6.2 — Session, node identity and updater reliability

## Sessions
- Preserve authorized sessions for seven days, with the existing five-minute renewable token cycle.
- Expired and revoked sessions transition directly to the login form, with no false empty-dashboard or intermediate error view.
- Ignore late 401 responses from requests authenticated with a previous token after a successful renewal.
- NPMX peers sharing a management endpoint accept each other's newly issued JWTs after pairing and matching-version upgrade, using an HKDF-derived, purpose-specific key from the existing secure cluster pairing secret. Standalone nodes retain RSA-signed tokens, and old RSA tokens remain locally verifiable.
- A user may have to sign in again once after both paired nodes finish upgrading, especially if the browser holds a token issued before v1.6.2.

## Real Linux host identity
- Mount the Docker host's /etc/hostname read-only in SQLite, MySQL and PostgreSQL Compose deployments.
- Prefer the verified physical hostname; fall back to the matching host-updater marker or NPM_NODE_HOSTNAME override.
- In-app upgrades retain the host's existing Compose configuration. The native host updater refreshes its hostname marker automatically after a healthy upgrade, without modifying custom Compose files. New Compose installations also receive the read-only hostname mount.
- Never confuse a Docker container ID with the host machine's hostname.

## Updater resilience
- Bound release metadata checks to eight seconds and cap GitHub response sizes.
- Show update status and recovery controls even when GitHub release metadata cannot be retrieved.
- Show the actual remote-check error instead of falsely claiming the installation is up to date.
- Continue using the existing systemd-native updater, with no secondary/helper containers.

## Notes for NPMX upgrades
Upgrade each node sequentially, and verify health between nodes. Complete both upgrades before evaluating cross-node session persistence; v1.6.1 cannot verify the new shared JWT format. Session validity still respects user revocation, password changes, token expiry and cluster pairing boundaries.
